newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mark down as French vote spurs fears of weak euro.
newsitem.headline: Mark down as French vote spurs fears of weak euro.

text.p: A stunning parliamentary election win by France's Socialist-led opposition caused a wave of mark sales in Tokyo on Monday, as fears mounted that Europe's planned single currency, the euro, would get off to a weak start, dealers said.

"Even if European economic and monetary union (EMU) starts on time, the image of a weak euro has been further confirmed by the French election...which led to mark selling," said Junichi Kodama, managing director and head of corporate sales at Chase Manhattan Bank in Tokyo.
The dollar, bought for its safe-haven status, strengthened against the mark, hitting a high of 1.7170 marks in morning trade in Tokyo, up sharply from 1.7056/61 marks in late New York on Friday.
The German currency also dipped to about 67.66 yen in the morning from its New York close of 68.18 yen, although it recovered modestly to about 67.85/88 yen at 0323 GMT.

"The mark was sold against other major units as the victory by the Socialist-led opposition underscored the market belief that the EMU will start on schedule, but with more relaxed fiscal criteria," said a chief trader at a major U.S. bank.
The Socialist Party is committed to launching a single currency, but is demanding a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty and early membership for Italy, Spain and Portugal in EMU.

Hidemitsu Terry Terasawa, manager of the Foreign Exchange and Treasury Division at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said that the Socialists' failure to win an absolute majority could trigger further problems as they must placate political allies such as the Communist Party, which wants a fresh referendum on the single currency.
"For France, it is the worst-case scenario," he added.

With 567 constituencies declared, the Socialists and their non-Communist allies, including the Green party, fell short of an absolute majority in the 577-member National Assembly. To rule they will need the support of the Communist Party, which won 38 seats.
"Now the market is going to focus on whether (French Socialist party leader Lionel) Jospin will stick with his campaign pledge," Terasawa said.

Jospin, who is expected to be appointed prime minister later on Monday, said on Sunday the people had voted for a change of direction in European policy, but he did not call into question the planned single European currency.

In European crosses, the French franc lost further ground against the mark and there was market talk that the Bank of France sold the mark for the franc at slightly below 3.3800 francs in early Asian trading, traders said.
A dealer at a French bank in Tokyo said a jump in the mark to 3.39 francs is possible if French bonds and stocks are sold heavily later in European trading.
The mark was quoted at 3.3835/40 at 0435 GMT.
